title: Digging sticks (juwal)

identification.basis: The dictionary's juwal 'yam or digging stick' is the word Roth wrote as tchu-al for the Bloomfield digging stick in 1904. Roth's section on digging sticks and Anderson's Bloomfield account, with Idriess's description from before the First World War, give the tool itself.

summary: The **[juwal](word:juwal)** is the yam stick, and the dictionary gives it the same word as the yam: a staff of strong, heavy wood, two to five feet long, flattened to a spade at one end and hardened in the fire, that a woman carried everywhere and would not lend [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:roth1904] [ref:anderson1996]. Roth, who recorded it at the Bloomfield as *tchu-al*, called the digging stick 'essentially women's implements, carried about by them, and employed for digging up "yams," roots, etc.', and noted that its 'almost universal pattern' made it 'admirably suited for the purpose': the thin spade end 'easily finds its way down when stuck into the ground, and not only offers increased leverage in loosening the soil, but also assists in shovelling it to the surface' [ref:roth1904]. Ion Idriess, who lived at Bloomfield before the First World War, saw it do much more: 'as a digging stick for uprooting vegetable foods, as a prodder and lever for forcing small animals (snakes, lizards, birds) from log or burrow or tunnel in river bank ... Primarily, though, it is a digger of yams ... About five feet long, a heavy, well-seasoned staff of hardwood, it tapers at one end to a point, and this makes a very efficient tool' [ref:anderson1996]. By 1873 an iron rod was doing the job at Bloomfield, and in the 1970s 'a shortened and sharpened crowbar' [ref:anderson1996].

infobox.label: Who
infobox.value: A woman's tool and her own property; also her weapon

infobox.label: Size
infobox.value: 2–4 ft (Roth); about 5 ft (Idriess); heavy, well-seasoned hardwood

infobox.label: Tip
infobox.value: Flattened, spade-like, charred in the fire to harden; later a rod of iron or a knife blade cemented in

infobox.label: Timber
infobox.value: The harder mangroves, eucalypts and ironwood

infobox.label: For
infobox.value: Yams and roots; levering small animals from logs and burrows; water; fighting

sections.heading: Names
sections.body: **[juwal](word:juwal)** is 'yam or digging stick', one word for the food and the tool; Roth's Bloomfield name for the digging stick, *tchu-al*, is the same word in his spelling [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:roth1904]. **[bakal](word:bakal)** is 'dig', and also 'stab, prick' [ref:hershberger1982]. Roth found that 'the local names for digging-sticks are apparently independent of the timbers employed', and set the Bloomfield *tchu-al* beside the Cape Bedford *dirm-ba* and *gana*, the Pennefather *kirtru*, and the Princess Charlotte Bay *kallara*, which 'is the name of a "yam"' there too [ref:roth1904]. The things it digs: **[kawu](word:kawu)** 'yam'; **[wukay](word:wukay)** the hairy yam that 'must be cooked, ground and leached before eating'; **[biyangkal](word:biyangkal)**, roasted, ground and leached 'before it can be safely eaten'; **[wawukuna](word:wawukuna)** 'long wild yam'; **[bambayal](word:bambayal)** 'a long thin variety of yam'; **[banjay](word:banjay)**, 'small and round ... roasted in the fire, ground up and eaten. Given to the child to make it talk'; **[kalkurr](word:kalkurr)**, **[warrabuka](word:warrabuka)** and **[wubali](word:wubali)**, species of wild yam; and **[ngakun](word:ngakun)**, a yam that is also the flame tree whose flowering 'signals the time when the scrub hen eggs are in season' [ref:hershberger1982]. See [yams](entry:yam).

sections.heading: The tool
sections.body:
Roth's description, from across North Queensland with the Bloomfield name attached [ref:roth1904]: 'Made of some strong and heavy timber, between 2 and 4 feet long, the attenuated spatulate extremity easily finds its way down when stuck into the ground, and not only offers increased leverage in loosening the soil, but also assists in shovelling it to the surface, when the operator exercises the usual to-and-fro movement. To harden the extremity it is often charred with fire. In the neighbourhood of civilisation the spatulate extremity has come to be replaced by a length of rounded scrap-iron, sometimes even a table-knife blade, firmly cemented into a handle.' A broken spear-tip might serve as a digging stick. 'The timber out of which digging-sticks are made comes from the harder species of mangrove, and eucalypt, and from "iron-wood" where generally available'; on the Endeavour River it was the mangrove *Scyphiphora hydrophyllacea*. 'The handle of the weapon is often to be seen decorated with red and white paint in bands, or one colour alone may just be smeared on indiscriminately'; Pennefather women fixed the paint with beeswax, and used honey as the medium for the pigment [ref:roth1904].

Idriess's Bloomfield stick was longer and pointed rather than spade-ended: 'About five feet long, a heavy, well-seasoned staff of hardwood, it tapers at one end to a point, and this makes a very efficient tool' [ref:anderson1996]. Anderson calls it 'one of the most important subsistence tools at Bloomfield' and records that 'the palm fibre dilly-bags and yam sticks for women and the net-bags, spear throwers and spears for men, were all considered personal items and would not normally be lent to others' [ref:anderson1996]. In the settled fights of the camp, 'men used fighting sticks and women used their yam sticks. ... There are several eyewitness accounts of women fighting using yam sticks' [ref:anderson1996]. Iron came early: in 1873 William Hann 'found in a camp at Bloomfield "pieces of iron, and amongst them a rod of the same metal, about three feet in length, evidently used as a yam stick"'; by 1904 iron or a table knife was being cemented into the end of a digging stick; and Cape Bedford was exporting iron digging-sticks along the coast [ref:anderson1996] [ref:roth1904] [ref:roth1910].

sections.heading: Digging stick, fighting stick, crowbar
sections.body:
- **The yam stick** is a woman's: heavy, spade- or point-ended, fire-hardened, carried from camp to camp [ref:roth1904] [ref:anderson1996].
- **The man's fighting stick** is a different thing, used in the same settled fights; a Bloomfield one is in the Australian Museum [ref:anderson1996] [ref:khan1993].
- **A broken spear** will dig in a pinch [ref:roth1904].
- **The pointed Wellesley Islands stick**, 'acicular', is the exception to the spade pattern [ref:roth1904].
- **The iron rod** of 1873, the knife-bladed stick of 1904, and the sharpened crowbar of the 1970s are the same tool in a new material; a crowbar is heavier than it needs to be and does not float [ref:anderson1996] [ref:roth1904].
- **The [adze](entry:axes-and-adzes)** hollows; the digging stick levers.

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body:
- **Yam country**: Anderson's yams 'grew in the sandy-soiled, open forest country, on the edges of swamps and on the river and creek banks' [ref:anderson1996].
- **The vine**: the long yam's climbing stem on a sapling, dying back in the dry, marks where to dig; see [yams](entry:yam) [ref:rfk-dtransversa].
- **Dug ground**: narrow deep holes beside a dead vine, and heaps of roots gathered 'ready for preparation' at a camp [ref:roth1904].
- **A log or bank being worked**: the prodder's job for lizards, snakes and birds [ref:anderson1996].
- **The stick itself**: polished handle, charred blackened tip, red and white bands [ref:roth1904].

sections.heading: Timber
sections.body: 'The harder species of mangrove, and eucalypt, and ... "iron-wood" where generally available' [ref:roth1904]. Roth's Endeavour River stick was a mangrove, and on the Pennefather an *Acacia*; any straight limb of a dense, heavy wood that will take and hold a fire-hardened edge is the right one [ref:roth1904].

sections.heading: What the stick gets at
sections.body: Underground is a store that only the stick opens. [Yams](entry:yam) and the other tubers 'through to November' on the sandy flats; the [zamia](entry:zamia) and the big roots that go to the [leaching](entry:leaching) pits; [witchetty grubs](entry:witchetty-grub) in the roots of the trees; [goannas](entry:goanna) in their burrows, lizards and snakes in logs, birds in tunnels in the river bank, which Idriess saw it lever out; freshwater [mussels](entry:mussels) in the sand of the pools; and water itself, dug for in a dry sand bed [ref:anderson1996] [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Seasons
sections.body: The yam stick's year is the dry: tubers and yams from the end of the wet through to November, the long yam dug when its vine has died back and marks the spot, the zamia from July [ref:anderson1996] [ref:rfk-dtransversa]. New sticks are cut with the other timber work after the first storms, and seasoned; Idriess's stick was 'well-seasoned' [ref:anderson1996]. See [the year on country](entry:seasons).

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
- Digging yams, roots and tubers: 'primarily ... a digger of yams' [ref:anderson1996] [ref:roth1904].
- Levering small animals from logs, burrows and bank tunnels [ref:anderson1996].
- Getting at water in sand [ref:anderson1996].
- A woman's weapon in the settled fights of the camp [ref:anderson1996].
- A walking staff and a carrying pole; the one tool that went everywhere with its owner [ref:anderson1996] [ref:roth1904].

sections.heading: Making and using a juwal
sections.body:
From Roth, Idriess and Anderson [ref:roth1904] [ref:anderson1996]:

1. **Cut a straight limb** of ironwood or a hard eucalypt, as thick as a wrist, between two and five feet long [ref:roth1904] [ref:anderson1996].
2. **Season it**: a green stick is light and bruises; Idriess's was 'a heavy, well-seasoned staff' [ref:anderson1996].
3. **Shape the working end** to a flat spade (Roth's 'attenuated spatulate extremity') or a point, with shell, stone or a knife [ref:roth1904] [ref:anderson1996].
4. **Harden the end** by charring it in the fire, and scrape the char back to hard wood [ref:roth1904].
5. **Paint the handle** in red and white bands if you like; the Pennefather women fixed the paint with beeswax [ref:roth1904].
6. **Dig** by stabbing the spade end down beside the yam, levering with 'the usual to-and-fro movement' to loosen the soil, and shovelling it up with the flat; follow the tuber down rather than pulling it [ref:roth1904].
7. **An iron end**: a length of rounded iron or an old knife blade cemented into a wooden handle was the 1904 version, and a cut-down sharpened crowbar the 1970s one [ref:roth1904] [ref:anderson1996].

Then the yams go to the [earth oven](entry:earth-oven), and the bitter and hairy ones through roasting, grinding and [leaching](entry:leaching) [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
- Snakes are among the things the stick levers out of logs and burrows; keep the stick between you and the hole, and know [snakes](entry:snakes) [ref:anderson1996].
- *Wukay* and *biyangkal* are poisonous until processed; the digging is the easy part of the yam [ref:hershberger1982].
- Do not dig at scarred trees, stone arrangements or any place that looks made; cultural heritage carries a duty of care under the *Aboriginal Cultural Heritage Act 2003* [ref:acha2003].
- Cutting a limb on someone's land is a matter for the Traditional Owners and the landholder; see each place below.

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body: The wooden *juwal* is a quick thing to make. Gathering on native title country is a right protected by section 211 of the *Native Title Act 1993* [ref:alrc]; how each determination words it is under each place below.

sections.heading: Language
sections.body: *[juwal](word:juwal)* 'yam or digging stick'; *[bakal](word:bakal)* 'dig; stab, prick'; *[kawu](word:kawu)* 'yam'; *[wukay](word:wukay)* 'hairy yam'; *[biyangkal](word:biyangkal)* a yam to be roasted, ground and leached; *[wawukuna](word:wawukuna)* 'long wild yam'; *[bambayal](word:bambayal)* 'a long thin variety of yam'; *[banjay](word:banjay)* a small round yam; *[kalkurr](word:kalkurr)*, *[warrabuka](word:warrabuka)*, *[wubali](word:wubali)* wild yams; *[ngakun](word:ngakun)* a yam, also the flame tree; *[jujabala](word:jujabala)* 'ironwood tree' [ref:hershberger1982].

locations.summary: On the Hann the yam stick's work is in the sandy woodland. Thaypan people's foods include 'bally yams that grow on a long stem, bush carrot and bush potato' [ref:fca-thaypan], and the Kuku Thaypan Elders' sandy mixed-tree country has 'a diverse understory of brachychiton and yams', with **Ku morteal**, the Cooktown ironwood, growing over them [ref:standley2019]. The oldest written record of yams being dug and prepared in this country is Roth's, from the Morehead and Musgrave rivers about 1900 [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: Yams and timber here
sections.body: The Elders' mixed-tree country, 'on slightly elevated light sandy soil', has bloodwood and **Ku morteal** (*Erythrophleum chlorostachys*, Cooktown ironwood) over 'a diverse understory of brachychiton and yams'; its trees and plants have uses 'in arts, crafts, weaponry, food, hunting and ceremony' [ref:standley2019]. Ironwood is the timber Roth names first for digging sticks, 'where generally available' [ref:roth1904], and here it is: the Atlas of Living Australia holds 50 Cooktown ironwood records, 1970–2026, in a box of about 90 × 85 km around the middle Hann, Laura and western Rinyirru. It holds only one record each of a yam (*Dioscorea bulbifera*) and of arrowroot (*Tacca leontopetaloides*) in the same box, both from 2012 [ref:ala-hann]; the Atlas records where collectors have been, not how many yams there are.

sections.heading: When to dig here
sections.body: In the Elders' fire calendar, 'Yam finished growth' is one of the signs, with the gum trees flowering and 'lillies and orchids growing', that the time for early burning has come [ref:standley2019]. Their fires are lit to spare the yams: one photograph shows 'a cool fire that has burnt the dead grass around the yams, enabling them room to spread' [ref:standley2019].

sections.heading: Yams and arrowroot on the Morehead and Musgrave (Roth, about 1900)
sections.body:
These rivers run, like the Hann, to Princess Charlotte Bay. What Roth saw there [ref:roth1901]:

**Round yam** (*Dioscorea sativa* var. *rotunda*, Morehead River):

1. Cut the rootstocks 'into halves or quarters' and wash them in a [bark trough](entry:bark-troughs).
2. Bake them 'in a hot ant-bed covered with tea-tree bark and earth' for about twenty minutes, until soft.
3. Put them in a grass [dilly bag](entry:dilly-bags) and squeeze it under water in a trough; the meal passes through, and the bag and what is left in it are thrown aside.
4. Let it settle, pour the water off, add more, and repeat 'some four or five times'.
5. Pour the watery meal down a piece of bark into a basin hollowed in the sand, so the water drains away. 'As soon as fairly dry it is eaten.'

**Arrowroot** (*Tacca*, Morehead and Musgrave rivers): the tubers were 'rubbed up against a rough stick' like a nutmeg-grater into a bark trough of water, squeezed through an infolded dilly-bag into fresh water, settled and washed, and the sediment 'cooked in hot ashes like a "damper"'.

See [leaching](entry:leaching) and [yams](entry:yam). These are what Roth saw about 1900, not tested recipes: ask the Traditional Owners which yams are safe and how.

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: The upper Hann is the Possum People's country and the middle and lower Hann are Thaypan country, under the Federal Court determinations of 2 November 2023 [ref:fca-possum] [ref:fca-thaypan]; downstream, Rinyirru is jointly managed by the Rinyirru Aboriginal Corporation and the Queensland Government [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture]. Native title holders may gather for personal, domestic and non-commercial communal needs without the licences others need [ref:nta1993]. Anyone else digging or cutting timber needs the Traditional Owners' permission.

locations.summary: On the open sandy [woodland](entry:woodland) of [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters), where the long [yam](entry:yam) *Dioscorea transversa* is recorded, it is the first tool to make [ref:ala-dtransversa] [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Yam country here
sections.body: Anderson's yam country, sandy-soiled open forest by swamps, rivers and creeks, is the Karma Waters sand country exactly [ref:anderson1996] [ref:re-woodland].

sections.heading: Timber here
sections.body: At Karma Waters that means the [ironwood](entry:ironwood), **[jujabala](word:jujabala)**, which is recorded within 60 km of the homestead, and the hard eucalypts of the [woodland](entry:woodland): the ironbarks and bloodwoods [ref:ala-erythrophleum] [ref:re-woodland] [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: What it digs here
sections.body: The Australian Museum has freshwater [mussels](entry:mussels) from the Mitchell near Karma Waters, the kind that live in the sand of the pools [ref:ala-mussel].

sections.heading: Permission here
sections.body: Cutting a limb on the station is a matter for the lessee's permission [ref:kw-about].

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: The yam country the *juwal* was made for is the sand of the Mitchell. Gathering is recognised in the Western Yalanji determinations [ref:wyac2020].

locations.summary: The *juwal* is the Bloomfield's yam stick, and most of what is written about it above comes from the Bloomfield [ref:roth1904] [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: In the late 1970s at Bloomfield 'bush vegetables were dug using mainly steel digging sticks, often a shortened and sharpened crowbar', and the yams were still processed [ref:anderson1996].
